item.title: Building a DIY Meraki Z3 with WireGuard and OPNsense
item.description:
I want to host a SaaS business. I also have a lot of old hardware sitting around that would totally be capable of handling that. VPSs start cheap, but can balloon in cost fast. However, I’m not too keen on exposing my residential IP for a business venture OR renting expensive-to-scale cloud infrastructure.

Anyway, I work in IT. I get exposed to a lot of weird lil devices. One of them happens to be the Cisco Meraki Z3: a little teleworker box. You plug internet into one ethernet port, you get a VPN-protected connection out the other. It’s as if you’re plugging into a switch on a remote site. Everything behind it comes out on the internet from the hub’s address.

Wait a minute. You can find cheap VPS rentals with static IPs and pretty high monthly transfer limits. Also Wireguard kicks ass. What if…

The design

📋
 [LAN devices] ── [OPNsense box] ══ WireGuard (full tunnel) ══ [Debian VPS] ── internet
                  10.10.10.0/24      10.200.0.2                 10.200.0.1
  • Hub: a Debian VPS running WireGuard at 10.200.0.1. It NATs everything out to the internet.
  • Appliance: OPNsense at 10.200.0.2 on the tunnel, with the remote LAN (10.10.10.0/24) behind it.
  • Other peers: my own devices join the same tunnel (for example 10.200.0.3) so I can reach things on the remote LAN through the hub.

The goals were:

  1. All remote-LAN traffic leaves via the VPS, and the remote ISP’s address never shows up.
  2. If the tunnel dies, nothing falls back to the local connection.
  3. The OPNsense GUI is not reachable from the LAN side or from the VPS.

Part 1: The VPS

I wanted the VPS to have as small an attack surface as possible: SSH disabled, a firewall that only allows the WireGuard port, and automatic updates (with automatic reboots). This separation also greatly reduces the chance that those auto updates break stuff.

📋
systemctl disable ssh
systemctl stop ssh
ufw reset
ufw default deny incoming
ufw default allow outgoing
ufw allow <WG_PORT>/udp
ufw enable
apt update
apt install wireguard -y

Generate the server keypair, and keep the private key to yourself:

📋
umask 077
wg genkey | tee /etc/wireguard/server.key | wg pubkey > /etc/wireguard/server.pub

Then /etc/wireguard/wg0.conf:

📋
[Interface]
Address = 10.200.0.1/24
ListenPort = <WG_PORT>
PrivateKey = <SERVER_PRIVATE_KEY>
PostUp = sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1; iptables -A FORWARD -i wg0 -j ACCEPT; iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o enp1s0 -j MASQUERADE
PostDown = iptables -D FORWARD -i wg0 -j ACCEPT; iptables -t nat -D POSTROUTING -o enp1s0 -j MASQUERADE

# opnsense appliance
[Peer]
PublicKey = <OPNSENSE_PUBLIC_KEY>
AllowedIPs = 10.200.0.2/32, 10.10.10.0/24

# my workstation
[Peer]
PublicKey = <WORKSTATION_PUBLIC_KEY>
AllowedIPs = 10.200.0.3/32

A few notes:

  • enp1s0 is my VPS’s uplink. Many guides say eth0. Check yours with ip route | grep default. If the name is wrong, the MASQUERADE rule matches nothing and all the tunnel traffic silently goes nowhere.
  • The OPNsense peer’s AllowedIPs includes the remote LAN. That’s how the server knows 10.10.10.0/24 lives behind 10.200.0.2, and it’s what lets my other peers reach the remote LAN through the hub.
  • FORWARD -i wg0 -j ACCEPT also covers peer-to-peer traffic, since that arrives on wg0 and leaves on wg0.

Enable it at boot:

📋
systemctl enable wg-quick@wg0
systemctl start wg-quick@wg0

Part 2: OPNsense

Recent OPNsense versions have WireGuard built in, so there’s no plugin to install. This is what I configured, in order.

WAN

  • Interfaces > WAN: disable Block private networks.
  • Firewall > Rules > WAN: add a rule to allow admin access to This Firewall.
  • System > Settings > Administration: set the listen interface to WAN only, so the GUI isn’t served on the LAN side at all.
  • Firewall > Settings > Advanced: disable the anti-lockout rule, since I’m managing access with explicit rules instead.

The tunnel

VPN > WireGuard > Instances

  • Name: Main
  • Tunnel address: 10.200.0.2/24
  • Generate a keypair and paste the public half into the VPS’s [Peer] block.
  • Peers: Main

VPN > WireGuard > Peers

  • Name: Main
  • Public key: the VPS’s public key
  • Allowed IPs: 0.0.0.0/0 (this is what makes it a full tunnel)
  • Endpoint: <VPS_IP>, port <WG_PORT>
  • Keepalive: 25

Interfaces > Assignments: add wg0 and name it WG. Then open it and tick Enable.

The route you must not forget

With a peer that has 0.0.0.0/0 as allowed IPs, OPNsense will happily try to send the WireGuard handshake packets into the tunnel they are supposed to establish, causing an infinite loop of failure. On my setup this showed up as follows. I could ping the VPS’s tunnel address when I listed explicit subnets, but pinging it failed the moment I switched to 0.0.0.0/0.

The fix is a more specific route for the VPS’s public address so it always leaves via the real WAN:

System > Routes > Configuration

  • Network: <VPS_IP>/32
  • Gateway: WAN_DHCP
  • Description: WireGuard endpoint bypass

Longest prefix wins, so /32 beats 0.0.0.0/0.

Outbound NAT

Out of the box, OPNsense only NATs traffic leaving the WAN. For this setup you also need to masquerade LAN traffic leaving through the WireGuard interface, otherwise the VPS sees 10.10.10.x source addresses it has no route back to.

Firewall > NAT > Outbound: switch to Hybrid, then add a rule:

  • Interface: WG
  • Source: the LAN network (10.10.10.0/24)
  • Translation: Interface address
  • Description: Masquerade LAN out WireGuard

Firewall rules

LAN

  1. Block, destination WAN net, moved to the top. This is my “don’t leak out the regular connection” rule.
  2. Block, TCP/UDP, destination This Firewall, port 443. This stops the GUI being reachable from the LAN.
  3. The default Allow LAN to any rule below those.

WG

  1. Block, destination This Firewall, TCP port 443, moved to the top. This is “no GUI or SSH access from the VPS”. If the VPS is ever compromised, it shouldn’t be a stepping stone to the firewall.
  2. Block, destination WAN net.
  3. Pass all, described as Allow inbound from WG tunnel. Return traffic from the internet needs this to get back in.

Rules are evaluated top-down and the first match wins, so the blocks have to sit above the broader allows.

Housekeeping

  • System > Settings > Miscellaneous: set the thermal sensor to coretemp so the dashboard shows CPU temperature.
  • System > Settings > Cron: add two jobs on Tuesdays. One runs the automatic firmware update, then at 01:00 another reboots the box.

A caveat on the “kill switch”

WAN net in OPNsense means the subnet of the WAN interface, not “the internet”, so rule 1 above is a weaker kill switch than it looks. A sturdier approach is a pair of floating rules on WAN: pass UDP to the VPS endpoint, then block everything else outbound. Whichever you use, test it by taking the tunnel down on purpose and checking that a LAN client can’t reach the internet, and that curl ifconfig.me doesn’t return your home address.

Footnote: e(vil)1000

I ended up doing a lot of troubleshooting when I was trying to get my virtualized workstation connected to the VPN. Long story short: I was using the e1000 virtual device as a workaround to get Moonlight working, and that device was mangling MTU values. If you’re curious, you can expand the section below, but it won’t be super relevant for most. Regardless: test your setup with the simplest possible connection, because the complexity Proxmox introduced wasted me a lot of time. (But I learned a lot!)

Show more

Everything above worked: LAN clients got the VPS's address and the tunnel was stable! The last thing I wanted was to reach the Proxmox host on the remote LAN (10.10.10.2) from my workstation (10.200.0.3), over the tunnel, through the hub.

Symptoms:

  • ping 10.10.10.2 worked.
  • SSH worked, roughly. Sessions would sometimes freeze, and some commands that produced a lot of output hung.
  • The Proxmox web GUI on port 8006 just timed out.

If you've done networking for a while, you've already guessed "MTU". I did too, eventually. Here's the order I tried things in.

Theory 1: Proxmox's firewall

Proxmox has its own firewall, so I added an accept rule for the WireGuard subnet, then turned the firewall off completely. No change. (The config files for the firewall didn't even exist, so it was never configured in the first place.)

Theory 2: pveproxy is broken

curl -k https://localhost:8006 hung over an SSH session but worked from the physical console. That looked bad, but ss -tlnp showed pveproxy happily listening on *:8006, and the service was healthy. The SSH weirdness turned out to be a symptom, not a cause, and I'll get to that.

Theory 3: the packet capture

This is where it got interesting. tcpdump on the Proxmox side during a failed request showed:

  • The TCP handshake completes.
  • The client sends its TLS hello (418 bytes). Fine.
  • Proxmox replies with a 1340-byte segment, then a 530-byte one.
  • The client SACKs the second segment ({1341:1871}) over and over, and never acknowledges the first.
  • Proxmox retransmits the first one until the client gives up.

The small packet gets through, and the big one disappears. Classic.

Theory 4: MTU and MSS, everywhere

So I set MTUs on every device along the path and clamped MSS with iptables -t mangle on Proxmox, first with --clamp-mss-to-pmtu and then hardcoded values. I changed the WireGuard MTU on both ends to 1420, then on the workstation to 1320 and lower. The SYN-ACK did show the lower MSS after clamping, which proved the clamp was working. But the failing segment just got smaller (1340, then 1280) and still vanished.

A test ping made it look like path MTU discovery was broken:

> ping -l 1400 10.10.10.2
Request timed out. (x4)

I spent a while adding ICMP pass rules to OPNsense. They were not the problem, and a capture on OPNsense showed the oversized echo request arriving and the reply leaving with no complaint.

Theory 5: Windows

Windows reported the WireGuard adapter's MTU as around two billion, which sent me down a path of Set-NetIPInterface, disabling LSO, checksum offload, and a handful of netsh tweaks. That did break things further: at one point the tunnel was half-dead and tcpdump saw nothing at all.

The actual cause

Then I tried the same tunnel config from a different device, and the GUI loaded instantly.

My "workstation" is a Windows VM running on another Proxmox host, and I had given it an Intel e1000 virtual NIC. The emulated e1000 has well-known problems with TCP segmentation offload and checksum handling, and they show up exactly like this: small packets fine, large ones silently eaten, SACK stalls. Switching the VM's NIC model to VirtIO fixed it. Everything I'd done to MTUs, MSS, ICMP rules, and Windows offload settings was compensating for a problem that was never in the network.

Lessons

  1. Test your tunnel from a second, independent client before you go down a diagnostic rabbit hole. If I'd done this at the start I'd have saved hours.
  2. Say what your client actually is. I was describing a "workstation" without mentioning it was a VM, and so was whoever was helping me debug. The most important fact was missing.
  3. Don't use the Intel e1000 NIC model in Proxmox for anything you care about. Use VirtIO.
  4. "Ping works, SSH mostly works, big transfers hang" means MTU or segmentation problems. The SSH freezes weren't a Proxmox quirk. They were the same dropped-big-packet problem showing up in a different place.
  5. Capture on both sides of a hop. Seeing that the server was sending a full segment and the client never ACKed it narrowed the problem to "somewhere in between", even though "in between" turned out to include the client's own virtual hardware.
  6. Undo your experiments. If you went through the same detour, flush the mangle rules on the Proxmox host (iptables -t mangle -F), restore vmbr0 and the physical NIC to MTU 1500, and set the tunnel MTU back to a sane default.

Claude’s Suggestions

  • Tightening the WAN-side admin rule. For now it’s open to the upstream network and I’d like to restrict that.
  • A real kill switch with floating rules rather than relying on WAN net.
  • Monitoring: Grafana with Telegraf on the OPNsense box, so I get the dashboard that the Meraki gives you for free.

…and one more suggestion from me: I’d really like to find a system that checks for zero-day CVEs, cuts off internet if not yet patched, and repeatedly checks for updates until patched. But that’s a bigger project for another time.

item.title: Convert Old PC into Dedicated DVD Player
item.description:
Had to do this at work and figured I’d share my notes here. Any usefulness these computers can get after their expected life is less money wasted.

  1. Download LibreElec (including the USB creator) and make yourself a flash drive.
    • The default download links may be blocked by your network. You can find active mirrors here.
  2. Before booting the flash drive, you’ll want to go into the BIOS and disable networking.
    • On the computer I did this with (Dell Optiplex 3040), the setting to disable the network adapter was located under System Configuration > Integrated NIC > Disabled.
    • This doesn’t prevent people from plugging in a USB ethernet adapter but at least it makes it clear that it’s not supposed to be connected to the internet.
    • You might also want to set a BIOS password to prevent people from re-enabling it.
    • Also would recommend putting an uncrimped RJ45 in as a dummy plug. May need a bit of “percussive maintenance” to get in.
  3. Let the flash drive boot automatically or type installer and press Enter to continue. It might seem like it hung for a second but it is actually loading.
  4. Install it. It will use up the whole disk, no special partitioning or anything.
  5. Remove the USB.
  6. You’ll need to manually choose the reboot option once it’s finished.
  7. Keep hitting Next until you’re done with the welcome dialog.
  8. Now to configure some options:
    • Interface
      • Skin
        • Configure skin...
          • Main menu items
            • Turn off EVERYTHING in this section.
    • System
      • Audio
        • Audio output device: Change to whatever it needs to be.
    • Player
      • Discs
        • Attempt to skip introduction before DVD menu: On
          • If this option doesn’t show up, make sure Advanced mode or higher is selected in the bottom left corner.
  9. Go back to the main menu.
  10. Insert a DVD.
  11. Click Play Disc.
  12. Make sure the audio works. If not, check your audio settings.

Notes

The reason we don’t enable DVDs playing automatically is because it triggers a pop-up menu. People have been complaining about this for well over a decade but it doesn’t seem like Kodi cares. Oh well!

item.title: Notes: Setting Up Postfix on Windows
item.description:
(Notes primarily for my own reference.)

I want this so that I don’t have to set up a bunch of generic accounts for each machine, seems like it could very quickly spiral into a maintenance nightmare. Keep in mind that most Google Workplace orgs will block these for many reasons. Somehow, Microsoft doesn’t seem to care.

I settled on this docker image after trying the following:

  • The built in SMTP server on Windows Server 2022: Just flat-out doesn’t work to the point where attempting to send crashes the service outright. Seriously, fuck this thing. What a ginormous waste of time.
  • Postfix under WSL(2): WSL(2) is ALSO not supported on Windows Server because Microsoft fucking hates you.

Once you’ve got Docker set up:

📋
docker run `
	--name postfix `
	-e "ALLOWED_SENDER_DOMAINS=localhost" `
	--restart always `
	-p 1587:587 `
	boky/postfix

When sending emails, make sure to set the server to localhost:1587.

Bonus!

You may be operating this from a network where the MX records aren’t working for one reason or another. You can manually specify the IP address to route the emails to using the following:

📋
docker run `
	--name postfix `
	-e "ALLOWED_SENDER_DOMAINS=localhost" `
	--restart always `
	-p 1587:587 `
	-e "POSTFIX_disable_dns_lookups=yes" `
	--add-host [DOMAIN NAME]:[MX RECORD IP] `
	boky/postfix

You can find the MX record IP using a tool like MXToolbox.

item.title: Notes: Migrate Debian Linode to Proxmox
item.description:
These are old notes from like 2022, but the process is probably still mostly the same. Let me know if there are any issues.

  1. Download your Linode’s disk image.
  2. Import the disk image to an existing VM in Proxmox. Make sure the VM is configured for BIOS boot, not UEFI.

Our Linode image only contains the system partition, that is to say what is normally /dev/sda1 is instead the entire disk, /dev/sda. We’ll need to copy the entire disk’s data to a partition on a new disk so that we can fit a partition layout and therefore a bootloader.

  1. Create another disk of the same size and attach it to the VM.
  2. Download, attach, and boot GParted Live.
  3. Initialize partition table of other disk using MBR format.
  4. Create a partition filling the entire disk and apply the changes.
  5. Time for the terminal!
📋
# Get root shell
sudo su
# Copy the data!
dd if=/dev/sda of=/dev/sdb1 status=progress
# Time to do some config editing...
mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt
# In fstab, comment out the line pointing to the swap partition.
nano /mnt/etc/fstab
# Remove the command line parameters from the GRUB config.
nano /mnt/etc/default/grub
# Install the GRUB bootloader
grub install --boot-directory=/mnt/boot /dev/sdb
# The output it provides is gonna be a bit screwed up for now.
# Edit the file below to replace all `root=/dev/sda` with `root=/dev/sda1`
nano /mnt/boot/grub/grub.cfg

poweroff
  1. Remove the assigned ISO and original system disk image, then boot. You should be able to get to your normal shell.
  2. More terminal!
📋
# Get root again...
sudo su
# Fix the bootloader for real this time
update-grub
# Fix your network interfaces (https://wiki.debian.org/NetworkConfiguration)
nano /etc/network/interfaces
# Fix your APT sources by replacing all instances of `mirrors.linode.com` with `deb.debian.org`
nano /etc/apt/sources.list
# Empty this file and fix your DNS nameservers. You should probably point it to your router if you don't know what you want to put here.
nano /etc/resolv.conf
# Off to the races!
apt update
apt upgrade

item.title: Notes: Linux
item.description:
Random notes for Linux. Primarily for my own reference.

Scripting

📋
# Change Dir to Script Dir
cd "$(dirname "$0")"

Personal Utilities

📋
echo "Deepseek API Key:"
read key_deepseek
cd ~
mkdir bin
cd bin
curl https://zyedidia.github.io/eget.sh | sh
echo "1" | ./eget -a static.tar.gz zyedidia/micro
./eget sigoden/aichat
cd ~
cat << EOF >> .bashrc
export PATH=$PATH:~/bin
export EDITOR=micro
alias ai="aichat -e"
alias l="ls -la"
alias e="micro"
fixperms() {
  dir="$1"
  user="$2"
  group="$3"

  [ -d "$dir" ] || {
    echo "usage: fixperms <dir> <user> <group>" >&2
    return 1
  }

  chown -R "$user" "$dir" &&
  chgrp -R "$group" "$dir" &&
  chmod -R u+rwx,g+rwx,o-rwx "$dir"
}
EOF
mkdir -p ~/.config/aichat/
cat << EOF > ~/.config/aichat/config.yaml
# see https://github.com/sigoden/aichat/blob/main/config.example.yaml
model: deepseek:deepseek-chat
clients:
- type: openai-compatible
  name: deepseek
  api_base: https://api.deepseek.com
  api_key: $key_deepseek
EOF
exec bash

(My) Ideal Debian VM Setup

Serial Access

📋
# Enable serial console
systemctl enable serial-getty@ttyS0.service

General

📋
timedatectl set-timezone America/New_York
apt update
apt upgrade -y
# Enable automatic upgrades
apt install unattended-upgrades apt-listchanges sudo curl git -y
echo "Unattended-Upgrade::Automatic-Reboot-WithUsers \"true\";" > /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/52unattended-upgrades-local

With Docker

📋
curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh
docker run --detach --name watchtower --restart unless-stopped --volume /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock containrrr/watchtower

With SMB Share

📋
#!/bin/bash
export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
export NEEDRESTART_MODE=l
apt install cifs-utils -y
echo "Linux username: "
read linux_username
echo "SMB Username: "
read smb_username
echo "SMB Password: "
read smb_password
mkdir /media/share
printf "username=$smb_username\npassword=$smb_password" > /root/sharecreds.txt
printf "\n//10.10.10.4/home /media/share cifs credentials=/root/sharecreds.txt,uid=$linux_username,gid=$linux_username,file_mode=0770,dir_mode=0770,noperm 0 0\n" >> /etc/fstab
systemctl daemon-reload
adduser $linux_username
echo "*/1 *  * * *  mount -a" | crontab - # Hack
mount -a
